short: Queen Zenobia turned a client kingdom into a breakaway empire spanning Egypt and the Levant before Aurelian crushed it.
full:
Palmyra, a wealthy caravan city on Rome's eastern frontier, had governed much of the region on Rome's behalf since its ruler Odaenathus checked Persian advances after Valerian's capture in 260. When Odaenathus was assassinated in 267, his widow Zenobia ruled in the name of their son Vaballathus and, from around 270, pushed Palmyrene forces into Egypt and much of Asia Minor, minting her own coinage and eventually claiming imperial titles for herself and her son independent of Rome.

The emperor Aurelian marched east in 272, defeating Zenobia's armies before besieging and capturing Palmyra itself; Zenobia was taken prisoner while trying to flee. A second revolt in 273 provoked Aurelian to destroy the city outright. The episode marked the empire's furthest loss of territory during the third-century crisis and, alongside the Gallic Empire's fall the same year, the restoration of a single Roman state under one ruler.
